title: The Gazelle Skin: a Corsair's Apprenticeship, a World Map, and the Siege at Hormuz
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Gelibolu, birth on the Dardanelles
stops.date_confidence: approximate; sources give only c. 1465 to 1470, with no attested day, month, or year
stops.campa: On the Ottoman shore of the Dardanelles, in a town whose whole business is ships, a son is born to Haci Mehmed and named Muhiddin Piri. No register of the birth survives: no day, no month, and a year the sources will only place somewhere between 1465 and 1470. The town is the whole of what is attested. The strait outside the door carries every fleet moving between the Aegean and the Sea of Marmara, and the shipyards work within earshot of the house, so the boy grows up among hulls coming down the water and men on the quay who can say where each one is bound.
suggested_refs: The shipyards and straits traffic of Ottoman Gelibolu, the naval town of his childhood
sources: Svat Soucek, Piri Reis and Turkish Mapmaking after Columbus

stops.name: Gelibolu harbor, aboard his uncle's ship
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is given by the biographical tradition, tied to the death of his parents
stops.campa: His parents are dead, or the tradition holds that they are, and the boy goes aboard the ship of his uncle Kemal Reis, a corsair captain working out of this same harbor. The apprenticeship is not an education in charts. It is boarding actions, prize crews, coastal raids, weather read off a rail in the dark, and what a cargo fetches in a friendly port. The uncle is already known on both sides of the sea. The nephew is one more hand aboard, roughly sixteen years old, and he will not come off the water again for thirty years.
stops.quote: We sailed on the Mediterranean and fought the enemies of our religion mercilessly.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, cited in Gregory McIntosh, The Piri Reis Map of 1513 (2000), p. 6
suggested_refs: The corsair fleet of Kemal Reis, operating out of Gelibolu before its entry into formal Ottoman service
sources: McIntosh, The Piri Reis Map of 1513 (2000)

stops.name: Malaga, the guns turned on the besiegers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month of his squadron's action is not recorded
stops.campa: Granada is dying and Malaga is under siege. Kemal Reis brings his squadron under the walls of the Alcazaba and turns his guns seaward onto the Christian forces investing the port, one Muslim power's ships firing in support of another's last cities in Spain. Piri is in his early twenties and has been at sea six years already, watching a siege lost from the water. The year is attested; the month of his squadron's action is not. The relief fails. Malaga surrenders in August, and the people of the city are sold.
suggested_refs: The siege of Malaga, 1487, and the Ottoman naval support sent to the Emirate of Granada

stops.name: Ibiza, the salt pans and the captives
stops.date_confidence: span; the raiding years run roughly 1487 to 1492 and no single visit is dated
stops.campa: For six years the fleet works the western sea: the Spanish and French coasts, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, the Balearics. Near Mallorca eleven of his companions are killed in a fight. What he sets down forty years later, in the sailing directions, is smaller than that and more useful. At Ibiza, salt being loaded, and Turkish and Arab captives working the pans. In the Gulf of Mahon on Menorca, a freshwater spring beside a fig tree. Off Mallorca, rivers and olive oil. On Cabrera, rabbits.
suggested_refs: The Balearic chapters of the Kitab-i Bahriye, drawn from firsthand observation during the corsair years

stops.name: Almeria, ferrying the expelled
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the harbors used are not named in any source, and this pin stands for the Spanish coast generally
stops.campa: Granada has fallen and Spain is expelling its Jews. Bayezid II orders his corsairs to make themselves ferries, and Kemal Reis's ships cross and recross to carry Muslim and Jewish families out of Spain to North Africa. Piri sails in the evacuation fleet in his twenties. The same hulls that took prizes off this coast a year ago are carrying refugees off it now, on an order out of the palace. No source names a single port used on either shore, and this pin stands for the Spanish coast at large. How many people the fleet moved is not recorded either.
suggested_refs: Bayezid II's order to evacuate Muslims and Jews from Spain, 1492

stops.name: Sapienza, off Methoni: the battle of Zonchio
stops.date_confidence: attested; the battle is fought over four days between 12 and 25 August
stops.campa: Off the island of Sapienza the Ottoman fleet meets the Venetians in four days of fighting, the first sea battle anywhere decided by cannon mounted in ships. Kemal Reis has been in the sultan's formal service since 1495, when the palace answered his piracy with a commission rather than a punishment, and Piri Reis commands one hull in his squadron. How many hulls were present is not agreed. Accounts of his life give some 270 Ottoman ships against 150 Venetian; accounts of the battle itself give 260 against 95.
suggested_refs: The battle of Zonchio, 12-25 August 1499, first naval engagement decided by shipboard cannon

stops.name: Methoni, the Venetian fortress taken
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; Navarino falls in the same season, is retaken by Venice in December 1500, and is seized finally in 1501
stops.campa: Modon, Venice's fortress on the Messenian coast, falls to the Ottoman fleet, and Navarino falls in the same campaign season; Venice takes Navarino back in December and loses it again the following year. Piri Reis serves through all of it as a captain under his uncle. The work has changed shape: sieges, supply trains, and the slow reduction of stone walls, in place of the quick prize taken at sea and sold in a friendly port. Whether he preferred the one to the other he never says.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman-Venetian war of 1499-1503 and the fall of Modon and Navarino

stops.name: Off Valencia, the captive and the chart
stops.date_confidence: contested; the map's own marginal note places the capture near Valencia in 1501, while some accounts move it to 1502, the year of his return to Constantinople
stops.campa: Raiding the Spanish coast, the Ottomans take a sailor who says he has sailed with Columbus. From him Piri Reis obtains, by his own later account, a chart of the western ocean that had belonged to Columbus himself, together with parrot feathers and black stones out of the new lands. He is a corsair captain in his thirties. The exact water is unrecorded, open sea somewhere east of Valencia. The map's own margin puts the capture in 1501; some accounts move it to 1502, which is the year he returns to Constantinople.
stops.quote: A Genoese infidel, his name was Colombo, he it was who discovered these places.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, marginal note on the 1513 world map, Section V, trans. Yusuf Akcura (1935)
suggested_refs: The longest marginal inscription of the 1513 map, describing the Spanish captive and his chart

stops.name: Constantinople, the arsenal on the Golden Horn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: After fifteen years in the western sea the ships come home to the capital and tie up at the arsenal on the Golden Horn. Piri Reis is a man in his thirties with a chest of captured charts, notes on every harbor between Gibraltar and the Aegean, and a reputation made inside another man's. Kemal Reis is the admiral, known at court and answerable to the sultan. The nephew is a captain in his squadron. For the next eight years the record of his movements thins almost to nothing.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman naval arsenal at Kasimpasa on the Golden Horn

stops.name: Tripoli, the last sight of Kemal Reis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: At the Red Castle above the harbor of Tripoli, uncle and nephew see each other for the last time, on the return from a campaign in the Maghrib. Spain will take the port later in the same year and hold it for the emperor. Nothing marks the parting as final; there is no leave-taking in the record, only two sets of orders. Kemal Reis is to carry aid on toward Egypt. Piri Reis turns his own ship east, and the two wakes separate somewhere off the African coast.
suggested_refs: The Red Castle (Assai al-Hamra) at Tripoli, taken by Spain in 1510

stops.name: Off Samos, the storm that takes his uncle
stops.date_confidence: contested; accounts give 1510 and 1511 alike, the only fixed point being that news of the drowning reaches Cairo by February 1511
stops.campa: Kemal Reis is lost with his ship in a storm off Samos while carrying supplies toward Egypt. Neither the name of the ship nor the number of men lost with him is recorded. The year is not settled either: accounts give 1510 and 1511 alike, and the one fixed point is that news of the drowning reaches Cairo by February 1511. Piri Reis has sailed under this man since childhood and has been introduced to sultans and admirals as his nephew. Years later he writes the man's epitaph into a book of sailing directions meant for working pilots.
stops.quote: Many men go off thinking they will return: those who do not are those who knew little about where they were going. Behold Kemal Reis: he left intending to return but failed and sank at sea.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, Kitab-i Bahriye, cited in Christine Isom-Verhaaren (2022), p. 98
suggested_refs: The passage of the Kitab-i Bahriye in which Piri Reis eulogizes his uncle

stops.name: Gelibolu, the chest opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of his withdrawal from active service; the compilation runs to 1513
stops.campa: He goes home to Gelibolu and stops sailing. He is roughly forty-five. Out of the sea chest come twenty-odd charts and world maps, eight geographical treatises, an Arabic map of India, four newly drawn Portuguese maps of Asia, and the sheet he says came from Columbus. Twenty years of gathering, nothing yet assembled. In the same room he begins setting down, harbor by harbor, the sailing directions that will become the Kitab-i Bahriye. The compiling runs on through 1513.
suggested_refs: Piri Reis's working library of captured and inherited charts at Gelibolu, 1511-1513

stops.name: Gelibolu, the map finished in Muharram
stops.date_confidence: attested; the map is dated Muharram 919 AH, corresponding to March 1513
stops.campa: In Muharram of 919 he finishes a map on gazelle skin: the Atlantic, the coasts of Europe and Africa, the Caribbean drawn hard against Asia as Columbus believed it lay, and the South American coast running south along the edge of the sheet. He is copying, and says so in the margin, naming every source he used and claiming none of the discovery for himself. About a third of the sheet will survive. The eastern half is lost, and no copy of it is known to exist.
stops.quote: From about twenty charts and Mappae Mundi... from eight Jaferiyes of that kind and one Arabic map of Hind, and from the maps just drawn by four Portuguese... and also from a map drawn by Colombo in the western region I have extracted it.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, marginal note on the 1513 world map, Section VI, trans. Yusuf Akcura (1935)
suggested_refs: The surviving fragment of the 1513 world map, Topkapi Palace Museum Library

stops.name: The Rio de la Plata, where the vellum ends
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the pin marks the approximate latitude at which the surviving fragment's South American coast breaks off, not a recorded place on the map
stops.campa: The South American coast on the parchment runs south past the Brazilian shore to roughly the latitude where a great river mouth opens into the Atlantic. There the surviving fragment ends, cut or torn, and the drawn coastline swings east along the bottom of the sheet into a landmass the map does not name. The mainstream reading is that this eastward turn is Terra Australis, the theoretical southern continent posited by Ptolemy and drawn on most maps of the century.
stops.quote: The coasts and islands on this map are taken from Colombo's map.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, marginal note on the 1513 world map, Section V, trans. Yusuf Akcura (1935)
suggested_refs: The southern edge of the surviving 1513 fragment, where the Atlantic coastline turns east
sources: McIntosh, The Piri Reis Map of 1513 (2000)

stops.name: Kasimpasa, the timber ship and the robe of honor
stops.date_confidence: approximate; usually placed around 1515, with some accounts giving 1516
stops.campa: Hayreddin Barbarossa, wanting a tie to the new sultan, sends a captured ship loaded with wood up to the capital and gives Piri Reis command of the delivery. Selim I takes the prize and answers it with two galleys and a robe of honor. There is no ceremony beyond that and no document of appointment: a cargo accepted at the arsenal gate, two hulls handed back, a coat. He is in the sultan's service now rather than his family's. Most accounts place the delivery around 1515, some at 1516.
suggested_refs: Hayreddin Barbarossa's overture to Selim I, delivered by Piri Reis, c. 1515

stops.name: Alexandria, the harbor closed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the campaign of 1516-1517
stops.campa: The Ottoman army is taking Egypt from the Mamluks by land, and Piri Reis commands the ships that close the sea in front of Alexandria so that nothing reaches the harbor. The blockade belongs to the campaign of 1516 and 1517, and it is the first time his own career and imperial policy run on the same line exactly. The fleet he serves is cutting a Mamluk sultanate off from the Mediterranean; on the far side of the same country, Portuguese fleets have been working the Indian Ocean for nearly twenty years.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman naval blockade of Alexandria during the conquest of Mamluk Egypt

stops.name: Cairo, the map given to Selim I
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the conquest; the exact occasion and place of the presentation are not recorded
stops.campa: Cairo falls and the empire acquires Egypt, the Red Sea, and the guardianship of the pilgrimage road. Somewhere in the aftermath Piri Reis puts the gazelle-skin map into the hands of Selim I. It is the last certain sighting of the parchment for four hundred and twelve years. Nothing records what the sultan said of it, whether it was ever unrolled at court, or by what route it travelled from Egypt to a shelf in the palace library at Istanbul and lay there unread.
stops.quote: The hand of this poor man has drawn it and now it is constructed... By reducing all these maps to one scale this final form was arrived at.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, marginal note on the 1513 world map, Section VI, trans. Yusuf Akcura (1935)
suggested_refs: The Ottoman conquest of Egypt, 1517, and the presentation of the 1513 map to Selim I

segments.name: Mutiny, Rhodes, and the Book of Navigation

stops.name: Chios, the castle taken from his own side
stops.date_confidence: attested to February by the diary of Marino Sanuto; the end of the revolt is undated
stops.campa: In February he is in open revolt. With other captains he lands 800 men on Chios, takes a castle, and seizes some four hundred of the sultan's own subjects; the Venetian diarist Marino Sanuto records the count. In May he is still out, raiding Euboea and the coast near Athens. Then the record stops. Why he broke with the fleet, on what terms he came back, whether anyone was punished for it: no source answers any of it, and by the Rhodes campaign of 1522 he is in Ottoman service again.
suggested_refs: Marino Sanuto's diaries, recording the captains' revolt and the landing on Chios, February 1518

stops.name: Topkapi Palace, the first Book of Navigation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, early in Suleiman's reign
stops.campa: Suleiman is newly on the throne, and Piri Reis offers him a book: roughly 130 chapters of sailing directions for the Mediterranean, written in the plain language of a man giving orders on a deck, with an argument for taking Rhodes attached at the end. No response of any kind is recorded. No gift, no post, no acknowledgement appears in any source. Working sailors copy it anyway, and more than forty later manuscripts of the Kitab-i Bahriye survive, carrying over five thousand maps between them.
stops.quote: [S]ome knowledge cannot be known from maps; it must be explained.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, Kitab-i Bahriye, cited in Svat Soucek (2013), p. 138
suggested_refs: The first version of the Kitab-i Bahriye, c. 130 chapters, presented 1521

stops.name: Rhodes, the siege he had argued for
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the siege runs from June to December 1522
stops.campa: The conquest he recommended in writing is carried out, and he is in it. The siege runs from June to December. Suleiman takes Rhodes at the end of the year and ends two centuries of the Knights of Saint John on the island. The survivors are allowed to sail away under arms, and will settle at last on Malta and go on fighting the same fleet from there. Piri Reis wrote the argument for this siege and then served in it. What he did during the six months of it is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The siege of Rhodes, 1522, advocated in the first version of the Kitab-i Bahriye

stops.name: The Egypt voyage, Ibrahim Pasha asks about the charts
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the voyage; the pin marks the Egyptian destination, since the conversation happens at sea and no position is recorded
stops.campa: Grand Vizier Pargali Ibrahim Pasha sails for Egypt to put down the rebellion of Hain Ahmed Pasha, aboard the flagship Piri Reis commands. Somewhere on the passage the vizier asks about the ship's maps and charts, and the answers are good enough that he commissions the captain to enlarge his book into something a court can keep. The Kitab-i Bahriye records the conversation in its own epilogue. A question asked on a warship under way is the commission for the largest portolan atlas the Ottomans would make.
suggested_refs: The epilogue of the Kitab-i Bahriye, recording Ibrahim Pasha's commission during the 1524 voyage to Egypt
sources: Giancarlo Casale, The Ottoman Age of Exploration (2010), pp. 34-37

stops.name: Topkapi Palace, the two hundred and ten chapters
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: The second version goes to Suleiman: some 210 chapters, with harbor plans, anchorages, currents, freshwater sources, a long verse preface, and the first substantial Ottoman account of the Indian Ocean and the Portuguese voyages, Vasco da Gama's route to India among them. It is the more beautiful book, illuminated for a court that reads it as an object. Later scholarship judges it the less used one, since working sailors went on copying the plainer first version instead.
stops.quote: My friend, the Franks both read and write everything there is to know about the science of the sea. But do not suppose that they invented such knowledge on their own.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, Kitab-i Bahriye (1526 recension), cited in Giancarlo Casale (2019), p. 875
suggested_refs: The second version of the Kitab-i Bahriye, c. 210 chapters, presented to Suleiman in 1526

stops.name: Gelibolu, the second map and the blank parchment
stops.date_confidence: attested; the map is dated 935 AH, corresponding to 1528-1529
stops.campa: A second world map, drawn fifteen years after the first, covers the north Atlantic and the American coasts with new Spanish information: Greenland, Newfoundland, Florida, Hispaniola set correctly against Cuba as the earlier sheet had failed to do. Where he has nothing reliable he leaves the parchment empty rather than fill it with the sea monsters and guessed shorelines his contemporaries used for the purpose. Only a fragment of this map survives either.
stops.quote: Only the places known are sketched.
stops.quote_source: Piri Reis, legend on the 1528 world map, cited in Gregory McIntosh (2015), p. 313
suggested_refs: The surviving fragment of the 1528 world map, Topkapi Palace Museum Library

stops.name: Coron, the galley struck
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; Doria takes Coron in September 1532 and the counter-siege follows
stops.campa: Andrea Doria takes Coron for the emperor in September, and Piri Reis is sent against the Spanish garrison holding it with ten galleys and five fustas, fresh from a squadron of eight vessels hunting pirates in the Adriatic. He works in close under the walls. The fortress guns find his galley and he withdraws. The month of the counter-siege is not recorded. He is somewhere in his sixties and has been at sea for fifty years, still commanding a squadron, still not an admiral.
suggested_refs: Andrea Doria's seizure of Coron, 1532, and the Ottoman counter-siege

stops.name: Off Cyprus, the Contarina taken
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the position of the seizure is not recorded and this pin is offshore approximation
stops.campa: He takes the Venetian galley Contarina in the waters off Cyprus and refuses to hand back her cargo of precious stones, arguing that Muslim prisoners had been aboard her and that this makes the prize lawful. Where the seizure happened nobody wrote down, and this pin is an approximation offshore. Venice complains through its ambassador at the Porte, and what the Porte answered Venice has not come down. The peace between the two states has a year left to run.
suggested_refs: Venetian complaints to the Porte over the seizure of the Contarina, 1536

stops.name: Corfu, under Barbarossa's flag
stops.date_confidence: attested to the campaign season; the siege runs August to September 1537
stops.campa: The third Ottoman war with Venice opens and he hunts Venetian shipping the length of the eastern Mediterranean before joining Hayreddin Barbarossa's fleet at the siege of Corfu. The siege runs August into September. It fails, and the island holds. Between them the two men command the largest fleet in the Mediterranean: one a corsair a sultan made admiral, the other a corsair who arrived at court with a shipload of timber. Piri Reis is roughly seventy years old.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman siege of Corfu, 1537, under Hayreddin Barbarossa

stops.name: Topkapi Palace, the case of the Liona
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He attacks the Venetian ship Liona, kills twelve of her sailors, wounds twelve more, and takes captives off her. Venice presses the case at the Porte and asks for restitution. Piri Reis answers that the Venetians struck first, and Grand Vizier Rustem Pasha finds for him. What became of the captives taken off the Liona nobody wrote down. The fights he now has to win are settled in a room in Istanbul, by men he has never sailed with. He is close to eighty and still taking prizes.
suggested_refs: The Venetian complaint over the Liona and Rustem Pasha's ruling, 1546

stops.name: Galata, the house sold
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, before his departure for Egypt
stops.campa: Before leaving for Egypt to take up the Indian Ocean command he sells his house in the capital, and the garden with it, and the vineyard. Nothing in the record says why, and no letter of his survives from that year. He is roughly eighty years old and is being sent to a sea he has never sailed, four thousand miles from the one he has spent his life mapping harbor by harbor and shoal by shoal. Later readers take the sale for a man settling his affairs.
suggested_refs: The sale of Piri Reis's house, garden, and vineyard in Istanbul, 1547

stops.name: Suez, sixty sail for the Red Sea
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Yahudi Sinan is dead and the Indian Ocean command passes to Piri Reis: Hind Kapudani, admiral of the water the Portuguese have been closing for fifty years. On the twenty-ninth of October he sails from the arsenal at Suez with about sixty ships and stands south down the Red Sea toward Aden and Yemen. He is roughly eighty. The ocean ahead of him he knows from four Portuguese charts he once copied and from the chapters he wrote about it without having seen any of it.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman arsenal at Suez, base of the Indian Ocean fleet

stops.name: Aden, artillery in the hills above the bay
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the citadel's fall
stops.campa: He lands his troops beyond the reach of the city's guns, drags artillery up into the hills above the port, and brings the fleet into the crescent bay, so that Aden is under fire from the height and from the water in the same hour. The citadel falls on the twenty-sixth of February. The reasoning is the same that runs through his own harbor chapters, read from the other side: where a fleet can anchor, where guns can be got ashore, what ground commands the water. He is past eighty and commanding in person.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman capture of Aden, February 1548

stops.name: The Gulf of Aden, the relief fleet burned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the engagement site is unrecorded and this pin approximates the strait
stops.campa: A Portuguese force comes to retake Aden and finds the Ottoman fleet waiting for it. He runs the ships down, burns them, and takes their sailors prisoner, somewhere in the gulf toward the strait of Bab el-Mandeb, at a position nobody wrote down. The sultan rewards the Aden campaign with a timar said to be worth a hundred thousand silver coins, land in exchange for a harbor. For a year and a half the Red Sea is Ottoman from the arsenal at Suez to the open ocean.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman timar grant made to Piri Reis for the Aden campaign

stops.name: Suez, the second departure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Orders come from Suleiman to take Hormuz from the Portuguese, with Bahrain named as a second objective, and he sails from Suez with twenty-five galleys, five sailing ships, and about 850 soldiers. It is a small force for a fortress of that class. Rustem Pasha, the vizier who had backed him against Venice, is dismissed well after the fleet has left Suez, so the admiral is without a patron at court for most of the campaign and has no way of knowing it. The month is April.
suggested_refs: Suleiman's orders for the Hormuz campaign, 1552

stops.name: Muscat, a month under the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of the surrender
stops.campa: He besieges Muscat for a month and takes it, and the Portuguese garrison that surrenders is put on the benches to row the galleys that had captured them. The Gulf of Oman is open behind him and the season is still good. Ahead lies Hormuz, the island in the mouth of the Persian Gulf that the Portuguese have held for forty years and fortified against exactly this fleet arriving on exactly this errand. He has twenty-five galleys and eight hundred and fifty men.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman siege and capture of Muscat, August 1552

stops.name: Hormuz, the fortress that holds
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day the siege is lifted; the bombardment runs from September
stops.campa: He takes the town of Hormuz and cannot take the fortress. For weeks he batters it, and the Portuguese governor writes afterward that the walls were nearly down. His powder runs low. He asks Basra for reinforcements and Kubad Pasha sends none. On the ninth of October, warned that a Portuguese relief fleet is at sea, he lifts the siege. The fleet is real. Forty ships under Antao de Noronha, sent out by the governor of India, reach Hormuz a month after he has gone.
suggested_refs: The Portuguese governor's letter of 31 October 1552, describing the state of the Hormuz walls

stops.name: Qeshm, the plunder that convicts him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, immediately after the lifting of the siege
stops.campa: Withdrawing, he plunders the island of Qeshm. The Hormuz haul together with this one is reckoned afterward at well over a million pieces of gold, and the gold is the part of the campaign that will be remembered against him. Ottoman court histories treat the sack as the reason the siege was lifted, rather than as what a beaten fleet takes on its way out of a sea, and that reading reaches Istanbul before he does. Nothing in the record says what he thought he was doing at Qeshm, or whether the gold was ever counted.
suggested_refs: Ottoman court histories on the plundering of Qeshm and its use in the case against Piri Reis

stops.name: Qal'at al-Bahrain, the order not carried out
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the fleet's route past Bahrain is reconstructed from the campaign orders and the retreat to Basra, not attested at this place
stops.campa: Bahrain stands in the sultan's orders as the campaign's second objective, and the fleet passes it. No landing, no siege, no explanation entered anywhere in the record. The ships are heavy with plunder, short of powder, and followed by forty Portuguese sail somewhere astern. An admiral who has spent his life writing down what every harbor holds, where its water is and how its bottom lies, sails past this one without stopping. Whether he judged the island not worth the days, or his powder too low to spend on it, nothing survives to say.
suggested_refs: Qal'at al-Bahrain, the campaign's unattempted second objective
sources: Wikipedia, 'Piri Reis' (campaign orders compared against the retreat route)

stops.name: Basra, the governor refuses the rowers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month of his arrival is not recorded
stops.campa: He brings the fleet up the Shatt al-Arab to Basra and asks the governor for rowers to get the galleys home. Kubad Pasha, who sent nothing to Hormuz when reinforcements were asked for, refuses this too. Piri Reis leaves the greater part of his ships in the river, takes two, and goes on toward Egypt: an admiral crossing territory that is nominally his own empire's, without a fleet. The year is 1553. The month of his arrival at Basra is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman ships abandoned at Basra in 1553

stops.name: Cairo, the charge of bribery
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the Venetian letter reporting the charge; when the accusation was first laid is not recorded
stops.campa: He arrives in Egypt with two ships out of thirty and a quantity of gold, and the case against him takes its shape at once. Not failure: bribery. The claim is that he raised the siege of Hormuz because the Portuguese paid him to. A Venetian diplomatic letter of the fifteenth of November already reports both the charge and his replacement. The Ottoman historian Ibrahim Pecevi, writing later with the documents in front of him, thought the accusation could not be believed.
stops.quote: having raised the siege of the fortress of Hormuz because of bribery
stops.quote_source: Venetian diplomatic letter of 15 November 1553, cited in Wikipedia, 'Piri Reis'
suggested_refs: The Venetian diplomatic correspondence of November 1553 on the charges against Piri Reis

stops.name: Cairo, the beheading
stops.date_confidence: contested; 16 December 1553 is Idris Bostan's identification, older histories give 1554, and Turkish sources still print 1554
stops.campa: He is beheaded in Cairo on the sultan's order, somewhere between eighty-three and eighty-eight years old, since nobody knows his birth year well enough to say which. The date is disputed as well: 16 December 1553 is Idris Bostan's identification, while older histories and Turkish sources still print 1554. The place within the city is disputed and always has been. Of the grave, the Turkish accounts say only this: Mezarinin yeri bilinmemektedir, the location of his grave is not known.
stops.quote: although the bribe charge was implausible, the sultan deigned to believe it and issued an order of execution
stops.quote_source: Ibrahim Pecevi, Ottoman court history, cited in Wikipedia, 'Piri Reis'
suggested_refs: Idris Bostan's dating of the execution to 16 December 1553

stops.name: The Strait of Hormuz, the fleet left behind
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the interception point in the strait is not recorded
stops.campa: Seydi Ali Reis is sent down to bring the ships abandoned at Basra out of the Gulf and around into the Red Sea. The Portuguese intercept him in the strait his predecessor could not force, and the fleet is taken or destroyed there, hull by hull. It is one year since the admiral who led those ships into the Gulf was executed for failing to hold it, and this is the end of the Ottoman attempt on the Indian Ocean by main force. Nothing is sent to replace either the ships or the man. Where in the strait the interception happened is not recorded.

stops.name: Topkapi Palace Library, the bundle on the shelf
stops.date_confidence: attested to late 1929; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: The palace is being turned into a museum. The German theologian Gustav Adolf Deissmann, touring the collections, prompts a search of the library for overlooked geographical material, and the director Halil Edhem Eldem comes upon a disregarded bundle containing an unusual parchment map. The orientalist Paul Kahle reads the marginal notes, finds Columbus named there among the sources, and identifies the sheet as the surviving third of the world map of 1513.
stops.quote: a disregarded bundle of material containing an unusual parchment map
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Piri Reis map', on Halil Edhem Eldem's discovery, 1929
suggested_refs: The 1929 conversion of Topkapi Palace into a museum and the rediscovery of the 1513 fragment

stops.name: Ankara, the republic prints the facsimiles
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the Turkish Historical Society facsimile; Ataturk's interest dates from the rediscovery onward
stops.campa: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk takes a personal interest in the rediscovered parchment and sets facsimile publication and further research in motion. A republic twelve years old is looking for ancestors of its own, and finds a cartographer its sultans had executed. The Turkish Historical Society issues a facsimile of the second Kitab-i Bahriye in 1935. A four-volume colour photographic edition follows from the ministry in 1988, and the book goes into German, French, English, Italian, Greek, and modern Turkish.
suggested_refs: The Turkish Historical Society facsimile of the Kitab-i Bahriye, 1935

stops.name: Greenwich Island, the coast the map is said to show
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of Hapgood's book; the pin marks the Antarctic coast at issue, not any place Piri Reis knew
stops.campa: Arlington Mallery re-projects the 1513 map onto a grid of his own in 1956, and in 1966 Charles Hapgood publishes Maps of the Ancient Sea Kings, arguing that the landmass along the bottom edge is Antarctica surveyed before the ice, its drawn islands the buried mountains of Queen Maud Land. The geologist Paul Heinrich answers point by point: the ice sheet has stood for some thirty-four million years, post-glacial rebound is ignored, and the 1949 seismic survey behind the claim could not measure one percent of the area drawn. Von Daniken and Hancock repeat it regardless.
suggested_refs: Charles Hapgood, Maps of the Ancient Sea Kings (1966), and Paul Heinrich's geological rebuttal
sources: Hapgood, Maps of the Ancient Sea Kings (1966)

stops.name: Gelibolu, the bust on the waterfront
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the commemorative coin; the bust and the Karaman statue are undated in the reachable sources
stops.campa: A bust of him stands on the waterfront of the town where he was born, and a statue at Karaman, and in 1995 Turkey strikes a commemorative coin with his name on it. Neither the bust nor the statue is dated in the reachable sources. Ships carry the name as well: the research vessel K. Piri Reis, working the Aegean, and submarines. TCG Pirireis was an American boat, ex-USS Tang, leased in 1980 and decommissioned in 2004. TCG Piri Reis, a different hull entirely, was commissioned new in 2024.
suggested_refs: The Piri Reis bust at Gelibolu, the Karaman statue, and the 1995 Turkish commemorative coin

stops.name: Tuzla, the university opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Piri Reis University opens at Tuzla on the Asian shore of the Sea of Marmara, a private institution teaching navigation, marine engineering, and naval architecture to the officers of a merchant fleet. Four and a half centuries after a sultan had him beheaded for lifting a siege, the Turkish marine trains its watchkeepers in a school carrying his name, on a coast within a day's sail of the water where he first learned to read a shoreline off a moving deck.
